title: Fallback Synthesis and SLA Preservation Handbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This handbook consolidates guidance for synthesizing graceful fallbacks across the serving runtime while preserving customer SLAs. It covers the decision graph, kernel scheduling considerations, a profiling/playbook for investigating performance regressions that lead to fallbacks, an operational benchmarking protocol to validate fallback behavior, and concrete runbook steps for mitigation and postmortem.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce customer-visible SLA breaches by providing a repeatable playbook for when fallbacks, degradations, or variant swaps are triggered by runtime anomalies.
- Scope: Applies to all hosted and dedicated executions managed by the serving runtime (production fleets, canaries, and pre-production mirrors). Excludes private on-prem deployments where the customer owns local network/infra.

Intended audience:
- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers
- Runtime product owners and release engineers
- Observability/telemetry engineers and performance researchers

Key concepts and definitions:
- Fallback: Any automated or manual change that routes a request to a different model variant, region, or degraded execution path intended to preserve latency or error SLAs.
- SLA preservation target: Primary SLOs we attempt to preserve are p99 latency and availability per-customer route.
- Variant: Model quantization/size/compiled-kernel variant that is functionally compatible.
- Eviction vs fallback: Eviction is a resource reclaim action on a worker; fallback is a traffic-routing reaction at the decision layer.

SLO thresholds and mapping (operational values):
- Availability SLO: 99.9% over 30 days.
- Latency SLOs: p50 <= 50ms; p95 <= 120ms; p99 <= 320ms for short-chat routes (<=256 tokens). Long-form routes have route-specific p99s.
- Fallback trigger thresholds (examples):
  - p99 observed > 1.5x configured SLO for five consecutive 1-minute windows -> candidate fallback.
  - Error rate (5xx) spike > 3x baseline for 3 consecutive windows -> immediate evaluation.
  - GPU kernel queue depth > 85% for sustained 30s -> trigger conservative admission.

Fallback decision flow (high-level):
1) Detect anomaly: telemetry alert fires (latency/error/queue depth).
2) Correlate signals: match trace ids, kernel-level metrics (kernel latency, occupancy), and recent config changes.
3) Classify cause: kernel regression, model artifact, traffic surge, network degradation, or hardware failure.
4) Action selection: pick from the fallback catalog (model variant swap, route-level throttling, regional reroute, or degrade features).
5) Apply fallback with canary: route 5% -> fallback for 60s, observe p99 and error delta.
6) If successful: gradually ramp to 100% over 10 minutes.
7) If unsuccessful: rollback and escalate to incident channel.

Decision heuristics (rules of thumb):
- Prefer model-variant fallback when kernel CPU/GPU stalls or kernel timeout errors are observed.
- Prefer region-level reroute when network egress/ingress errors are correlated to region telemetry.
- Avoid functional-degrading fallbacks (e.g., remove tool-calls) for routes marked "high-fidelity" unless explicitly approved by product.
- Maintain conservative prefactors: use 1.5x–2x thresholds for latency-based fallbacks to avoid oscillation.

Kernel scheduling considerations during fallback:
- Preemptive eviction policy: mark fallback traffic as low-priority so kernels initiated by fallback traffic are subject to cooperative preemption.
- Kernel selection: when falling back to a quantized variant, ensure the kernel mapper chooses the relaxed-precision kernels with the same attention sharding to minimize KV-cache incompatibilities.
- KV cache handling: ensure session affinity mapping is preserved; if KV cache rehydration will introduce large cold-starts, prefer routing to a compatible variant that can share cache where possible.
- Admission throttles: apply admission tokens per-GPU to prevent fallback traffic from thrashing host queues.

Profiling playbook (quick triage):
1) Capture trace: enable 100% sampling on impacted route for a 5-minute window using trace tag: fallback-triage-<incident-id>.
2) Collect kernel-level histograms: per-kernel execution times, queueing durations, occupancy, and memory allocs for affected hosts.
3) Run lightweight reproducer: using the operational workload replayer, mirror a 10s slice of production traffic into a sandbox with kernel debug flags enabled.
4) Compare to baseline: use the last-successful-stable profile from the execution-profile-registry and compute delta percentiles.
5) Hypothesis checklist: kernel regression, bad kernel rollout, model weight mismatch, GPU thermal/driver regress, or system-level overload.
6) Apply mitigations: kernel rollback, model-variant swap, or admission controller limit.

CLI examples and snippets:
- Mark route for 5% fallback:
  redwoodctl routes update --route-id r-abc123 --fallback-variant quant-8bit --canary-percent 5 --canary-duration 60s

- Snapshot kernel histograms (host):
  curl -sS http://internal-metrics/hosts/host-23/kernelsnapshot | jq .histograms > /tmp/host-23-kernel.json

Benchmark protocol for validating fallback behavior:
- Objective: quantify the latency, error, and cost delta when switching to a fallback variant under representative load.
- Setup: use the operational-workload-simulator against a mirror stack with the same model catalog and kernel builds.
- Steps:
  1) Baseline: run 10m at expected steady QPS (S) and collect p50/p95/p99 and kernel histograms.
  2) Induce fallback: apply target fallback configuration (variant/region/quantization).
  3) Ramp workload: run a 30m scenario with 2x momentary spikes to simulate burst behavior.
  4) Measure: p50/p95/p99, error budget consumption, per-token GPU time, and per-request memory allocations.
  5) Pass criteria: p99 <= 1.2x baseline p99 and error rate increase <= +0.5 percentage points.

Configuration reference (examples):
| key | default | recommended for fallback testing |
|-----|---------|---------------------------------|
| admission.max_inflight_per_gpu | 1024 | 512–768 (reduce during fallback) |
| kernel.mapper.relaxed_precision | false | true for quantized variants |
| routing.canary.percent | 0 | 5–10 |
| kvcache.rehydrate_timeout_ms | 30000 | 15000 (for aggressive fallbacks) |

(When converting to the Confluence table UI, use the same three columns.)

Runbook: immediate mitigation steps (for oncall)
1) Acknowledge pager and post incident banner on #runtime-ops.
2) Gather: alert context, affected routes, recent releases (kernel/model), and top-5 affected hosts.
3) Execute safe fallback: route 5% to fallback variant using redwoodctl (see CLI example).
4) Monitor 60s canary: p99, 5xx rate, kernel queue_depth.
5) If canary improves SLA metrics -> follow ramp plan.
6) If canary fails -> rollback and execute isolation steps (drain hosts, cordon, and trigger host repair runbook).
7) Open incident with priority P1 and assign owners: runtime-oncall, kernel-author, model-oncall.

Post-incident checklist and postmortem triggers:
- Trigger a postmortem if SLA breach > 1 hour or customer-impacting errors exceed 1,000 requests.
- Include: timeline with kernel-level latency charts, decision rationale for fallback, and action items (e.g., kernel rollback automation).

Release notes and known issues matrix (short form):
- Release 2026.01.12: introduced conservative fallback orchestrator. Known: initial rollout underestimates KV cache rehydration cost for large sessions (work item assigned: PERF-876).
- Release 2025.10.30: relaxed_precision kernels added for several quantized variants. Known: a minority of kernels show 8–12% p99 regression under mixed-length sequences (mitigation: adaptive kernel selector flag).

Operational runbook annex (troubleshooting cheatsheet):
- Symptom: sudden p99 spike with no deploys
  - Check kernel histogram for long-tail spikes
  - If kernel spikes present -> try model-variant fallback to quant-8bit
  - If queue depth high and no kernel spike -> check admission throttles and increase preemption window

- Symptom: 5xx surge correlated to a recent kernel rollout
  - Rollback kernel bundle on affected hosts
  - Apply route-level canary to fallback variant

Ownership and escalation paths:
- Runtime oncall: first responder for detection, canary application, and short-term mitigation.
- Kernel team: authoritative owner for kernel rollbacks and performance fixes.
- Model onboarding: owner for validating functional compatibility of fallback variants.

Appendix: example incident timeline (fictional)
- 10:02 UTC: p99 alert fires for route chat-realtime-prod (observed p99 = 670ms).
- 10:03 UTC: oncall captures traces, correlates to kernel build k-7b2 which was rolled out at 09:58.
- 10:06 UTC: apply 5% fallback to quant-8bit variant; canary p99 -> 180ms.
- 10:20 UTC: ramp to 100% over 8min; monitor for regressions.
- 10:45 UTC: incident closed, follow-up action: pin k-7b2 rollout and queue a kernel hotfix.

Contact and feedback:
- For updates to this handbook, open a PR in the runtime-team-wiki repo and ping reviewers listed above.
- If you encounter a scenario not covered here, tag #runtime-ops with the label "fallback-gap" and file an architecture request.
